extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students/scholars of poetics and dramatic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic plots and for choices of diction/thought in dramatic poetry, derived from Aristotle's Poetics: plot construction, recognition, episodes, chorus, modes of expression, and figures of speech (metaphor, word-types, parts of language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best kind of recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The best recognition is that which arises from the incidents themselves, where the startling discovery is made by natural means (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These recognitions dispense with artificial aids (tokens, necklaces). Prefer recognitions that flow naturally from the plot rather than contrived signals; next-best are recognitions by process of reasoning; worst are arbitrary tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding false inferences in recognition scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions accompanied by false inference (a character drawing the wrong conclusion) can be effective but are inferior to natural recognitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Odysseus imagining the other would recognize him from the bow. Use with care to avoid implausible leaps by characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid visualization of the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing the plot and working it out with proper diction, the poet should place the scene as far as possible before his eyes to see everything vividly, as if a spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This visualization helps discover what is in keeping with the situation and prevents overlooking inconsistencies (example: the fault in Carcinus where a character's movement contradicted the staged situation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate gestures and acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Poet should work out the play with appropriate gestures because those who feel emotion are most convincing through gesture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional authenticity in acting increases conviction. Poetry implies either natural giftedness or inspired frenzy enabling the actor to assume characters convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline first, then fill episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether using an existing story or constructing one, the poet should first sketch the general outline and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a clear general plan (illustrated by Iphigenia): sketch the major sequence (disappearance, transport, seizure, recognition) before composing episodes and specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be relevant and appropriately short
rubrics_metrics.description: After the general plan, fill in episodes that are relevant to the action; in drama episodes should be short—these are the parts that give extension to epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure episodes contribute to the main action (example: Orestes' madness leading to capture and purification). Avoid extraneous episodes that do not serve the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part tragic structure: Complication and Unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication (from beginning to the turning-point) and Unravelling (from the beginning of the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define clearly the turning-point to good or bad fortune; design the sequence so that the Complication leads naturally to the Unravelling (examples: Lynceus, where presupposed incidents make the Complication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of tragedy: the Simple, the Complex (depending on reversal and recognition), the Pathetic (motives of passion), and the Ethical (motives ethical); exclude supernatural/lower-world kinds for ordinary practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poet should attempt to combine poetic merits from these kinds or, failing that, concentrate on the greatest number and most important traits; modern critics expect wide excellence across kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master both knotting (Complication) and unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity of a tragedy depends on plot—Complication and Unravelling must be the same; many poets tie the knot (Complication) well but unravel it badly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both skills (creating the Complication and resolving it) must be mastered; ensure coherence between the knot and its solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epic multiplicity of plots in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make a Tragedy into an Epic structure—avoid a multiplicity of plots; tragedy should select a portion rather than dramatize an entire epic tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic length allows each part to assume proper magnitude; in drama such multiplicity usually fails on stage (examples: dramatizations of the Fall of Troy or all of Niobe). Select appropriate scope and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversals aimed at moral-satisfying tragic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals of the action should aim to produce a tragic effect that satisfies the moral sense (e.g., the clever rogue outwitted, the brave villain defeated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reversal should feel probable enough to satisfy the audience while still achieving dramatic surprise; Agathon's view allows events somewhat contrary to strict probability if they serve effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole and share in the action (as in Sophocles), not mere interludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that are irrelevant to the subject (a feature criticized in later poets like Agathon); choral material should pertain to the piece's action and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought: aims and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (the 'what' produced by speech) includes proof and refutation, excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger), and suggestion of the like; it overlaps with rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought to elicit emotional and intellectual responses; consult rhetoric for techniques of argument and persuasion that support dramatic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should 'speak' themselves; speeches produce effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic incidents must be treated so they speak for themselves without verbal exposition; speeches should be used to produce the effects aimed at (emotion, persuasion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show rather than tell: if an incident conveys the necessary impression on its own, avoid redundant speech. When speech is necessary, craft it to produce the intended effect (pity/fear/etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of expression belong to declamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of modes of expression—what is a command, prayer, narrative, threat, question, or answer—belongs to the art of Declamation and not strictly to poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets need not be castigated for failing to distinguish every mode precisely; specialized declaimers handle fine distinctions of delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand basic linguistic units for poetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Language for poetry comprises parts: Letter, Syllable, Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion (case/tense/mood), and Proposition/Phrase; their properties (vowel, semi-vowel, mute; syllable composition) matter for metre and diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should be aware of phonetic and metrical behavior (long/short vowels, aspirated/smooth sounds, syllabic composition) because these affect rhythm and prosody; detailed metrical inquiry is distinct but necessary for verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of word-types and register
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be simple, double, triple, etc., and may be current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word-type and register appropriate to the poem's audience, character voice, and clarity. A 'current' proper word differs in effect from a 'strange' or 'ornamental' one; be mindful of local usages (σίγυνον example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: modes and permissable transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the transfer of an alien name by genus→species, species→genus, species→species, or by analogy (proportion). Metaphor may be qualified by adding the relative term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor by these recognized transfers; it may apply even if one term lacks a specific name (e.g., 'sowing the god-created light' for sun's rays). Metaphor can be extended, abstracted, or applied creatively; avoid obscurity if clarity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction virtue: clarity and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of diction is clearness and absence of baseness; clearest diction often comes from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that is clear and not lowly; proper names give greatest clarity though other resources (metaphor, varied word-forms) can be used when appropriate to tone and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot as test of sameness/difference
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging whether two tragedies are the same or different, the best test is the plot: identity exists where the Complication and Unravelling are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or comparing works, preserve both the Complication and its Unravelling; changing one but not the other changes the identity of the tragedy.
